common_name: Fire and Ice Hellebore (Winter Jewels Series)

planting.note: Set container divisions in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade, disturbing roots minimally.

directions: Fire and Ice is a hand-pollinated strain within the Winter Jewels Series bred by Northwest Garden Nursery, selected for warm-toned blooms that blend fiery red, apricot, and orange tones against icy pale edges or centers. As with other Winter Jewels strains, individual seedlings vary somewhat in exact pattern while sharing the strain's overall color theme, so plants are best chosen in bloom if a precise shade matters. Flowers nod from clumps of leathery, evergreen, palmate foliage from late winter into early spring, well ahead of most other perennials. Topdress yearly with compost, remove tattered old leaves before bloom, and avoid dividing the clump more often than every few years.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in fall into gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained soil, since this cross inherits some of H. thibetanus's intolerance of soggy ground.

directions: Pink Ice is an interspecies hybrid raised at Ashwood Nurseries in the English Midlands by crossing Helleborus niger with the deciduous, pink-flowered Chinese species H. thibetanus. The result opens pale pink buds that fade toward white as the nodding flowers age, combining the Christmas rose's refinement with an unusual blush tone rarely seen outside thibetanus-derived hybrids. It prefers a slightly drier, well-drained summer resting period than typical H. x hybridus and resents heavy, waterlogged clay. Grow in part shade with reliable winter moisture and summer drainage, and avoid disturbing the roots once established.

planting.note: Plant in spring into very sharply drained soil or a raised bed, since its H. vesicarius parent is a summer-dormant species intolerant of wet, humid summers.

directions: Briar Rose is one of the more unusual Ashwood Nurseries interspecies crosses, pairing the familiar Christmas rose Helleborus niger with the rare, summer-dormant Turkish species H. vesicarius, which dies back completely after setting its inflated seed pods. The hybrid shows an intermediate habit, retaining more foliage persistence than vesicarius alone while picking up some of that species' papery, balloon-like seed capsules. It demands gritty, fast-draining soil and a dry summer rest period, making it best suited to raised beds, troughs, or alpine house culture rather than an ordinary border. Collectors grow it chiefly for its novelty and the curiosity of its unusual parentage.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in fall or early spring into well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in a sheltered spot with some winter sun.

directions: Blackthorn Group was raised at Blackthorn Nursery in Hampshire, England, from the cross between Helleborus argutifolius and H. lividus, and it holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable garden performance. Its leathery, three-lobed evergreen leaves are marbled gray-green and strongly flushed with purple along the veins and margins, especially in cool weather, and clusters of cream flowers heavily tinted dusky pink open from late winter into spring. Unlike most Lenten rose hybrids it tolerates and even prefers a somewhat sunnier, drier site with sharp drainage, since it carries some of H. lividus's intolerance of wet, heavy soil. It is also shorter-lived than H. x hybridus and benefits from occasional replacement with self-sown seedlings, which often retain the attractive purple foliage flush.

common_name: Betty Ranicar Hellebore (Tasmanian Double White Lenten Rose)

planting.note: Transplant container divisions in fall into rich, humus-laden, well-drained soil in part to full shade; this vigorous strain forms large clumps and resents root disturbance once settled.

directions: Betty Ranicar arose as a chance double-flowered seedling discovered in a Tasmanian garden and named for the Australian hellebore enthusiast credited with finding and propagating it; the clone is documented in UK Plant Heritage's national hellebore collection records. It produces an abundance of large, fully double, ruffled, pure white flowers held above unusually big, glossy, dark green leathery leaves, making it a strong, vigorous grower even by Lenten rose standards. Clumps bulk up readily and flower heavily once established, tolerating a wider range of light than many double hellebores as long as soil stays humus-rich and evenly moist. Divide only when a clump becomes congested, since disturbance sets flowering back for a season or more.

common_name: HGC Silvermoon Hellebore (Gold Collection Pewter-Leaved Hybrid)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, disturbing roots as little as possible.

directions: HGC Silvermoon is a Gold Collection introduction within the Helleborus x ericsmithii group, the same niger-x-sternii lineage that produced HGC Champion and HGC Marlon, bred in Germany by Josef Heuger. Its leathery, toothed, pewter-gray-green leaves carry a distinctive silvery cast that sets it apart from greener-leaved relatives in the group, giving the clump year-round textural interest even before bloom. Rounded clusters of outward-facing flowers open white to pale green in late winter and age with soft pink tints as they mature over several weeks. Site it beneath deciduous shrubs for winter light and summer shade, topdress annually with compost, and trim away tattered old foliage just before the flowering stems emerge.

planting.note: Fall planting lets this short-lived species establish before its winter growth flush; set in lean, sharply drained soil.

directions: Chedglow is a foliage selection of the species Helleborus foetidus prized for its finely divided leaves splashed with gold variegation that is brightest on fresh spring growth and softens somewhat as summer heat arrives. Loose, drooping clusters of small, bowl-shaped cream-and-green flowers edged in maroon rise above the colorful rosette from late winter into spring. Like other stinking hellebores it is naturally short-lived and self-sows readily, so leave a few seedlings in place each year to keep a planting going, noting that variegation intensity can vary among self-sown offspring. Give it lean, sharply drained soil in light to moderate shade, since rich or waterlogged ground shortens its lifespan.
